titleStmt.title: Impacts of the Russia-Ukraine War on Global Food Security: Towards More Sustainable and Resilient Food Systems?
titleStmt.author: Tarek Ben Hassen
Hamid El Bilali

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Impacts of the Russia-Ukraine War on Global Food Security: Towards More Sustainable and Resilient Food Systems?

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the direct and indirect effects of the Russia-Ukraine war on global food security, assessed four months into the war
span.quote: Accordingly, this paper aims to investigate the Russia–Ukraine war’s direct and indirect impact on global food security.

span.label: how conflict-related disruption of the global food and fertilizer markets affects price and availability, and through which chains
span.quote: Understanding how conflict-related disruptions in global food and fertilizer markets might affect price and availability is critical for understanding the overall impact on global food security.

span.label: a review tracing four immediate consequences and four cascading indirect ones, and arguing that the severity is set by pre-existing rigidities in global food systems rather than by the war alone
span.quote: However, the consequences of the war on food security are being exacerbated by a variety of underlying rigidities, vulnerabilities, and inefficiencies in global food systems.

span.label: prediction
span.quote: Indeed, with the war doubtful to be resolved shortly, its influence on global resource markets will grow, as will the possibility of highly significant ‘ripple effects’ or ‘risk cascades’ on economies and society across the globe.

span.label: a food-price and food-availability shock propagating from a regional war into import-dependent countries far from it
span.quote: These effects may have swift and severe consequences in regions and industries far from the initial occurrence

span.label: a narrative review of the war's food-security impacts written four months in, drawing on FAO, Reuters and market reporting
span.term: a narrative review of the war's food-security impacts written four months in, drawing on FAO, Reuters and market reporting
span.quote: Further, four months into the war, its implications for food security suggest that this review is timely, urgent, and highly needed.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: ONE ROUTE CARRIES ALMOST EVERYTHING: 95% of Ukrainian grain leaves by sea from Odessa, Mariupol and Kherson, and all Black Sea ports were blocked - so a single chokepoint converts a regional war into a global supply event
span.quote: Indeed, 95% of Ukrainian grain exports are sent by sea via the ports of Odessa, Mariupol, and Kherson, which have suffered significant damage. In addition, all Black Sea ports have been blocked, shutting off most Ukrainian exports.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE ALTERNATIVE ROUTES ARE BLOCKED BY INFRASTRUCTURE, NOT BY POLITICS: the Ukrainian rail gauge differs from most EU nations', Constanta lacks the capacity, and building storage takes time - so rerouting is a multi-year problem presented as a short-term option
span.quote: Further, the Romanian port of Constanta lacks the capacity to manage the influx of Ukrainian crops

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: AN UNKNOWN END DATE DEFEATS THE INVESTMENT THAT WOULD FIX IT: because the embargo's duration is unknown, private capital will not fund the port and rail capacity the alternative routes need. The uncertainty is itself the obstacle
span.quote: In addition, because the embargo duration is unknown, attracting private investment for the infrastructure required for such alternatives is challenging

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: PRICE SIGNALS RUN BOTH WAYS AND THE PAPER SAYS SO: high fertilizer prices suppress farmers' use and simultaneously motivate producers to expand supply; high oilseed prices pull more planting into the US and EU. The net effect is not computed
span.quote: However, despite the negative adverse consequences of the war, some opportunities may arise and lessen these consequences.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE SHOCK LANDED ON A SYSTEM ALREADY STRESSED: prices were high before the invasion because of COVID-19 supply disruption, strong demand and poor harvests, so the war is an increment on an existing crisis rather than the origin of one
span.quote: Simultaneously, the war came at a bad time for global food markets because food prices were already high due to disruptions in the supply chain caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, strong global demand, and poor harvests in some countries.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: IMPORT CONCENTRATION IS THE TRANSMISSION MECHANISM: over 30 countries take at least 30% of their wheat from the two belligerents and at least 20 take over 50%, which is what makes distant countries price-takers on this war
span.quote: Indeed, over 30 countries rely on Russia and Ukraine for at least 30% of their wheat imports, while at least 20 countries rely on those two countries for more than 50% of their wheat imports, making them very sensitive to price shocks and/or supply shortages

span.label: the review was written four months into an unresolved war, so its forward claims are projections rather than observations - the paper says so in its own framing
span.quote: Further, four months into the war, its implications for food security suggest that this review is timely, urgent, and highly needed.

span.label: whether other exporters can fill the gap is stated as uncertain
span.quote: Consequently, according to FAO \ [19\], one-third of crops and agricultural land may not be harvested or cultivated by 2022.

span.label: the effect of sanctions on Russian output is conditional and unresolved - devaluation MAY impede productivity IF sustained, and no significant production interruption was predicted at the time of writing
span.quote: However, the financial sanctions imposed on Russia have resulted in a significant devaluation, which, if sustained, may impede productivity and development while eventually raising agricultural output costs

span.label: the counter-movements are reported without a net figure: increased plantings and expanded fertilizer production are set against the losses but never summed
span.quote: However, despite the negative adverse consequences of the war, some opportunities may arise and lessen these consequences.

span.label: seed availability is adequate for 70% of the predicted spring area, and the binding constraint is stated to be safe delivery rather than supply - a distinction that the aggregate loss figures do not carry
span.quote: For instance, although the available quantities of seeds (both local and imported) would be adequate to plant 70% of the predicted spring area, their safe delivery to farmers is a considerable challenge

span.label: the paper reports the counter-movement as well as the harm - higher oilseed and wheat prices pulling more planting into the US, EU and Canada, and higher fertilizer prices motivating producers to expand output
span.note: eliminates: a one-sided reading in which the war produces only losses - the paper reports the counter-movements (more oilseed and wheat planting, expanded fertilizer production), though it never nets them against the harm · outcome: partial
span.quote: However, despite the negative adverse consequences of the war, some opportunities may arise and lessen these consequences.

span.label: the pre-war baseline is stated rather than assumed: prices were already high from COVID-19 disruption, demand and poor harvests, so the war's contribution is not the whole of the observed rise
span.note: eliminates: the war as the sole cause of the price rise - prices were already high from COVID-19 supply disruption, strong demand and poor harvests before the invasion · outcome: held
span.quote: Simultaneously, the war came at a bad time for global food markets because food prices were already high due to disruptions in the supply chain caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, strong global demand, and poor harvests in some countries.

span.label: food security
span.quote: Accordingly, this paper aims to investigate the Russia–Ukraine war’s direct and indirect impact on global food security.

span.label: labor shortages
span.quote: Secondly, the war already prevented farmers from working in their fields, and the conscription and population displacement resulted in labor shortages.

span.label: conscription
span.quote: Secondly, the war already prevented farmers from working in their fields, and the conscription and population displacement resulted in labor shortages.

span.label: export restrictions
span.quote: Secondly, as seen during the 2007–2008 food crisis, many countries applied export restrictions, pushing up international market prices and worsening the crisis.

span.label: panic buying
span.quote: Thirdly, panic buying at both country and individual levels is another cascading affect of the war.

span.label: fertilizer prices
span.quote: Firstly, fertilizer prices are reaching near-record highs, which may severely limit usage and decrease yields.

span.label: yields
span.quote: Firstly, fertilizer prices are reaching near-record highs, which may severely limit usage and decrease yields.

span.label: wheat imports
span.quote: Indeed, over 30 countries rely on Russia and Ukraine for at least 30% of their wheat imports, while at least 20 countries rely on those two countries for more than 50% of their wheat imports, making them very sensitive to price shocks and/or supply shortages

span.label: sanctions
span.quote: However, the financial sanctions imposed on Russia have resulted in a significant devaluation, which, if sustained, may impede productivity and development while eventually raising agricultural output costs

span.label: SDGs
span.quote: The war may affect the progress toward the SDGs, especially SDG 1 (No Poverty), SDG 2 (Zero hunger), and SDG 12 (Responsible consumption and production).

span.label: risk cascades
span.quote: Indeed, with the war doubtful to be resolved shortly, its influence on global resource markets will grow, as will the possibility of highly significant ‘ripple effects’ or ‘risk cascades’ on economies and society across the globe.

span.label: the war's `impact` on food security - THE PAPER SEPARATES TWO KINDS AND THE DISTINCTION IS ITS STRUCTURE. IMMEDIATE impacts are physical and observed: exports stopped, ports blocked, farmers conscripted. INDIRECT ones are market-mediated and projected: fertilizer prices, export restrictions, panic buying. A reader who collapses them reads observations and forecasts as one kind of claim
span.quote: The paper highlights that the war resulted in immediate and far-reaching cascading consequences on global food security: Ukrainian exports have stopped, conscription and population displacement have caused labor shortages, access to fertilizers is restricted, and future harvests are uncertain.

span.label: the war as CAUSE - THE PAPER'S OWN THESIS IS THAT IT IS NOT THE CAUSE, IT IS THE TRIGGER. The consequences are said to be `exacerbated by a variety of underlying rigidities, vulnerabilities, and inefficiencies in global food systems`, which makes the war a stressor on a system already fragile - and it is why the conclusion is about food-system reform rather than about the war
span.quote: However, the consequences of the war on food security are being exacerbated by a variety of underlying rigidities, vulnerabilities, and inefficiencies in global food systems.

span.label: vulnerability - DEFINED HERE BY IMPORT CONCENTRATION, not by poverty or by proximity to the war: over 30 countries take at least 30% of their wheat from Russia and Ukraine and at least 20 take more than 50%. That is what makes the effects land `far from the initial occurrence`
span.quote: Indeed, over 30 countries rely on Russia and Ukraine for at least 30% of their wheat imports, while at least 20 countries rely on those two countries for more than 50% of their wheat imports, making them very sensitive to price shocks and/or supply shortages

span.label: builds-on → the 2007-2008 food-price crisis, whose export-restriction dynamic this paper says is repeating
span.quote: Secondly, as seen during the 2007–2008 food crisis, many countries applied export restrictions, pushing up international market prices and worsening the crisis.

span.label: distinguishes-from → the 2007-2008 food-price crisis as a precedent for this one
span.note: differs in: the starting condition - 2007-2008 followed a financial crash, whereas this shock arrives after two years of COVID-19
span.quote: Unlike the previous global food-price crisis, driven by the 2007–2008 financial crash, the current upheaval comes after governments and households spent two years coping with the COVID-19 pandemic—the most significant economic shock since World War II.

span.label: qualifies → accounts that treat the war as the cause of the food crisis; the paper holds that pre-existing rigidities and inefficiencies in global food systems are what turn the war into a crisis
span.quote: However, the consequences of the war on food security are being exacerbated by a variety of underlying rigidities, vulnerabilities, and inefficiencies in global food systems.

span.label: conscription —causes→ labor shortages
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.95
span.quote: Secondly, the war already prevented farmers from working in their fields, and the conscription and population displacement resulted in labor shortages.

span.label: fertilizer prices —causes→ yields
span.note: status: may severely limit · direction on the measure: reduces · strength of the relation: 0.9
span.quote: Firstly, fertilizer prices are reaching near-record highs, which may severely limit usage and decrease yields.

span.label: export restrictions —causes→ food security
span.note: status: as seen during the 2007–2008 food crisis · direction on the measure: reduces · strength of the relation: 0.9
span.quote: Secondly, as seen during the 2007–2008 food crisis, many countries applied export restrictions, pushing up international market prices and worsening the crisis.

span.label: sanctions —causes→ food security
span.note: status: would exacerbate · direction on the measure: reduces · strength of the relation: 0.85
span.quote: Furthermore, in April 2022, Russia vowed to limit agricultural and food exports to only ‘friendly’ countries in response to Western sanctions. The restriction would exacerbate the global food-supply shortfall

span.label: fertilizer prices —causes→ yields
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.8 — THE SAME PAIR IN THE OPPOSITE DIRECTION, AND BOTH ARE THE PAPER'S. High prices reduce farmers' USE of fertilizer and increase manufacturers' PRODUCTION of it. It is not a contradiction and it is not a converse-pair defect - the two edges have different subjects that the endpoint vocabulary cannot distinguish, which is why both carry a note rather than one being withdrawn. META's symmetry test will flag this pair; it should, and this is the answer.
span.quote: Additionally, high fertilizer prices will motivate fertilizer makers to boost production.

span.label: the war produced four immediate consequences - exports halted, labour shortages from conscription and displacement, restricted fertilizer access, and uncertain future harvests
span.quote: The paper highlights that the war resulted in immediate and far-reaching cascading consequences on global food security: Ukrainian exports have stopped, conscription and population displacement have caused labor shortages, access to fertilizers is restricted, and future harvests are uncertain.

span.label: the indirect chain runs through fertilizer prices reducing use and yields, export restrictions raising international prices, and panic buying at country and individual level
span.quote: Firstly, fertilizer prices are reaching near-record highs, which may severely limit usage and decrease yields.

span.label: the severity is attributed to pre-existing rigidities and inefficiencies in global food systems rather than to the war alone
span.quote: However, the consequences of the war on food security are being exacerbated by a variety of underlying rigidities, vulnerabilities, and inefficiencies in global food systems.

span.label: effects are expected to appear in regions and industries far from the war itself, through risk cascades
span.quote: These effects may have swift and severe consequences in regions and industries far from the initial occurrence
